implementation_notes: Swift has no ring buffer in the Foundation/stdlib; for a fixed, allocation-free numeric ring (audio frames via AVAudioEngine's tap, a telemetry ring) the construction is a fixed [Float] or UnsafeMutablePointer plus two indices, with the indices as ManagedAtomic from swift-atomics when the ring is shared across threads (the audio render callback and the main thread are different threads, so the ring genuinely needs atomics and a real-time-safe implementation - no allocation, no locks in the render callback). DispatchQueue and DispatchSemaphore are the higher-level blocking alternative if the producer can wait. For a bounded, blocking, multi-producer ring, a DispatchQueue-based or an OSAllocatedUnfairLock-guarded array is more appropriate. The ring's real-time constraint (the audio callback must never allocate or lock) is what makes the hand-written array the right answer on Apple platforms.
idiom_name: fixed [Float]/UnsafeMutablePointer ring with ManagedAtomic indices (swift-atomics); DispatchQueue/Semaphore as the blocking alternative
pitfalls: The audio render callback runs on a real-time thread: it must not allocate, take a lock, or block - so the ring is preallocated and lock-free, and a DispatchQueue or semaphore in that path is a priority-inversion bug.
ManagedAtomic is from the swift-atomics package, not the stdlib; the ring's indices need real atomics because the render and main threads are different threads.
Ordering is unchecked in swift-atomics: .relaxed on the release store (or .acquiring on the publish) compiles and fails on ARM.
The capacity must be a power of two for the mask; the indices must use wrapping arithmetic (&+, &-) so they do not trap at Int.max.
alternative: A DispatchQueue with a bounded backing buffer, or os_unfair_lock around a fixed array, when the producer can block
